title: Francevillian biota
summary: Black shales of the Francevillian B Formation near Franceville in southeastern Gabon, about 2.1 billion years old, hold more than 400 specimens from at least 45 levels in a 5 m section: pyritized lobate, elongated and rod-shaped forms, disks and microfossils. The authors read them as colonial organisms in an oxygenated sea, appearing after a rise in atmospheric oxygen.

uncertainty.note: "ca. 2.1 Ga" in El Albani et al. (2014); CNRS says "2.1 billion-year-old rocks". Years are Ga with no 1950 offset.

as_recorded.value: the ca. 2.1 Ga black shales of the Francevillian B Formation

where.modern_name: Franceville, Haut-Ogooué Province, Gabon (fossils from the Francevillian basin near the town)
where.historical_name: Francevillian basin, western equatorial Africa; no polities

paleo.not_applicable: Age is beyond the 1000 Ma limit of the MERDITH2021 plate model.

importance.justification: Among the oldest proposed macroscopic colonial organisms, tied by the authors to rising oxygen.

sources.title: The 2.1 Ga Old Francevillian Biota: Biogenicity, Taphonomy and Biodiversity (PLoS ONE 9:e99438)
sources.author: A. El Albani, S. Bengtson, D.E. Canfield, et al.

sources.title: Life Was Already Moving 2.1 Billion Years Ago
